covers.quote: Place a comma after adverbs and other introductory words
You don’t need a comma after an introductory word if the sentence is very short.

parts.quote: Yes, they went to the estimates hearing.
Goodnight, and good luck.
Actually, that's an interesting point.
Excuse me, should I come with you?
Today I went to work.

rules.quote: Use a comma after introductory words, such as greetings and adverbs, or when addressing someone.
rules.specification: ‘Very short’ is not quantified. A proposed operational interpretation is 5 words or fewer, accommodating the manual’s example ‘Today I went to work.’ This threshold is an interpretation, not a stated rule.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory word, greeting, adverb or expression addressing someone is not separated from the following main clause by a comma, outside the very-short-sentence exception.
when: Applies to introductory words and expressions separated from the main clause.
A comma is optional when the sentence is very short.
rules.why: G-1 selects the specific child check; G-3 records the short-sentence permission as an exception; G-4 consolidates the heading; E-4 makes the proposed threshold explicit.

covers.quote: Use a comma after phrases and clauses that change the whole sentence
Many introductory phrases can be moved to the end of sentences without changing the meaning. In these cases, you don’t need a comma before the phrase.
They should also have a comma after them if they start the sentence.
Use a comma after an introductory phrase that ends with a numeral and is immediately followed by another numeral. It doesn’t matter how short the sentence is.

parts.quote: During the meeting, we discussed Item 9.
We discussed Item 9 during the meeting.
During the meeting, we discussed item 9.
Although they were shaking and sweating, the firefighters were relieved to feel the first drops of a downpour.
Unless the consultation starts early, it will not finish on time.

rules.quote: Use commas after adverbial phrases and adverbial clauses.
rules.violation_condition: An introductory adverbial phrase or clause is not separated from the main clause by a comma, including a conditional clause or an introductory phrase ending in a numeral immediately before another numeral.
when: Applies when the adverbial phrase or clause starts the sentence.
Includes introductory conditional clauses beginning with words such as ‘if’, ‘unless’ or ‘until’.
A phrase moved to the end of the sentence without changing the meaning does not require a preceding comma.
An introductory phrase ending with a numeral immediately followed by another numeral requires a comma regardless of sentence length.
rules.why: G-1 selects the child check; G-2 consolidates conditional and numeral-ending cases; G-3 records the end-position exception; G-4 avoids a second heading rule.

covers.quote: Avoid this type of sentence structure because the string of numbers can be confusing.

parts.quote: There were 16.5 million people enrolled to vote in Australian elections on 18 April 2019.
On 18 April 2019, 16.5 million people were enrolled to vote in Australian elections.

rules.quote: Avoid beginning a sentence with a string of numbers and dates
rules.violation_condition: A sentence begins with a date or other numerical introductory phrase immediately followed by another number, producing a confusing string of numerical information.
when: Applies to the introductory numerical sequence described immediately below the heading.
A separating comma can make the sentence grammatical without removing this readability problem.
rules.why: The grain test separates the discouraged sentence structure from the required introductory comma; G-4 consolidates its restatement.

covers.quote: Set off non-essential clauses
Within a sentence, use a pair of commas to separate non-essential or supplementary information.
Generally, if you can take out part of the sentence and it is still grammatically correct, it should be between a pair of commas.
Don’t use commas if the clause is essential for meaning.
If you can remove the clause and your sentence means the same thing, it’s non-essential and should go between commas.

parts.quote: The committee, said the secretary, was incompetent.
The committee said the secretary was incompetent.
The business report, which the manager had edited, explained the agency’s strategy.
Introduced pests, such as varroa mite, threaten Australian honey production.
The report that the manager had edited explained the agency’s strategy.
Introduced pests from South Asia threaten Australian honey production.

rules.quote: Use commas around clauses that add information but aren’t essential to the meaning of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A supplementary, non-essential clause lacks its separating commas, or an essential clause is set off with commas as though it were supplementary.
when: A clause is non-essential if removing it leaves the sentence’s intended meaning unchanged.
A non-essential clause within a sentence requires both commas.
An essential clause must not be set off with commas.
rules.why: G-1 selects the clause child rather than a competing parent rule; G-2 keeps essentiality cases together; G-4 consolidates restatements; E-1 preserves both committee sentences as correct.

covers.quote: Use a pair of commas when you have 2 noun phrases next to each other that define the same thing.
You should be able to take out the noun phrase between the comma pair and still have a grammatically correct sentence.

parts.quote: The strike took place in Whyalla, South Australia, in June 2014.
The strike took place in Whyalla, South Australia in June 2014.
My colleague, Mx Lesley May, will exercise my proxy vote.
My colleague will exercise my proxy vote.

rules.quote: Place commas around nouns that define the same thing they follow
rules.violation_condition: A supplementary noun phrase following another noun phrase that identifies the same thing is not enclosed by the required comma pair.
when: The adjacent noun phrases identify the same thing.
The second phrase supplies non-essential information.
Removing the supplementary phrase leaves a grammatically complete sentence.
rules.why: G-1 selects the appositive child check; G-4 consolidates the body instruction and removal test.

covers.quote: Separate questions tagged onto a sentence

parts.quote: They’re not here, are they?
We’ll be reporting back, won’t we?

rules.quote: Use a comma before a question that is part of the sentence.
rules.violation_condition: A question tag attached to the end of a sentence lacks a comma separating it from the preceding statement.
when: Applies to a question tagged onto the end of a statement within the same sentence.
rules.why: G-1 gives question tags their own child check without also flagging them under the parent; G-4 selects the operative body sentence.

covers.quote: Use commas with the phrase ‘for example’
If ‘for example’ begins a sentence, it is an introductory phrase. Follow it with a comma.

parts.quote: Some colours, for example, are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish.
For example, some colours are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish.

rules.quote: Generally, use a comma before and after the phrase ‘for example’ in a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: The phrase ‘for example’ lacks a required separating comma: before or after a sentence-internal use, or after a sentence-initial use.
when: A sentence-internal parenthetical use generally takes a comma before and after the phrase.
A sentence-initial use takes a comma after the phrase.
When the phrase introduces a bullet list, the following punctuation is a colon rather than a comma.
rules.why: G-2 treats the phrase’s sentence position as a condition of one comma check; G-4 consolidates the heading and initial-position instruction.

parts.quote: Some colours are difficult for people with colour blindness to distinguish, for example:
red
green
orange
brown
blue
purple.

rules.quote: If you’re introducing a bullet list after ‘for example’, use a colon.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet-list lead-in ending with ‘for example’ lacks a colon after the phrase.
when: Applies when ‘for example’ introduces the following bullet list.
rules.why: The grain test separates the required list-introducing colon from the phrase’s comma check; E-3 keeps the lead-in and list items together.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas with Latin shortened forms

parts.quote: Exports of rare earths (e.g. lithium, europium) have soared.
Exports of rare earths (e.g., lithium and europium) have soared.

rules.quote: If you use Latin shortened forms, such as ‘e.g.’ and ‘i.e.’, don’t follow them with a comma.
rules.violation_condition: A Latin shortened form such as ‘e.g.’ or ‘i.e.’ is immediately followed by a comma.
when: Applies when a Latin shortened form is used.
rules.why: G-4 selects the body sentence, which specifies that the prohibited comma follows the shortened form.

covers.quote: Use commas to connect 2 or more principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’, ‘so’).
If they have different subjects, use a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
If 2 clauses share the same subject, you don’t need to repeat the subject or insert a comma before the conjunction.
The exception to this rule is when you have joined more than 2 principal clauses with the same subject.

parts.quote: The Senate debated the Bill at length, but the party whips eventually called for a vote.

examples.note: two clauses with a shared subject

parts.quote: The company closed its Perth office and sacked the chief financial officer.

examples.note: more than two clauses with a shared subject

parts.quote: The company closed its Perth office, sacked the chief financial officer, and opened a branch in Singapore.

rules.quote: Place commas between principal clauses joined together with a conjunction
rules.violation_condition: Principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction lack a required separating comma, either before the conjunction between clauses with different subjects or between more than 2 principal clauses sharing a subject.
when: Applies to principal clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction such as ‘and’, ‘or’, ‘but’ or ‘so’.
Clauses with different subjects require a comma before the coordinating conjunction.
Two clauses sharing a subject do not require the subject to be repeated or a comma before the conjunction.
More than 2 principal clauses sharing a subject require separating commas, including before the final conjunction.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the different-subject, shared-subject and multiple-clause cases in one check; G-3 records the shared-subject permission; G-4 consolidates body restatements.

rules.quote: Do not use this rule to create a sentence of more than 25 words.
rules.violation_condition: A sentence formed by joining principal clauses with commas and coordinating conjunctions contains more than 25 words.
when: Applies to sentences formed using the principal-clause joining rule in this section.
rules.why: The grain test separates sentence length from comma placement; unlike G-5 process advice, this instruction supplies a measurable property of the text.

covers.quote: Don’t use commas to ‘splice’ sentences

parts.quote: The report was finished last week, but the minister has not approved its release.
The report was finished last week, the minister has not approved its release.

rules.quote: Don’t use a comma to link 2 stand-alone sentences unless you use a coordinating conjunction.
rules.violation_condition: Two stand-alone sentences are joined by a comma without a coordinating conjunction.
when: A comma joining principal clauses is allowed when a coordinating conjunction supplies the link.
rules.why: G-4 selects the operative definition of the prohibited splice; the grain test separates an existing comma splice from a missing conjunction-boundary comma.

covers.quote: Separate items in lists of nouns or adjectives with commas
This rule applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments in bullet lists.

parts.quote: The delegation visited Brisbane, Canberra and Adelaide.
The consultation involved businesses, sole traders and not-for-profits.
The applicant was willing to learn, eager to work and well prepared.

rules.quote: Use commas between items in a sentence list.
rules.violation_condition: Adjacent items in a sentence list lack separating commas at ordinary item boundaries.
when: Applies to sentence lists and sentence fragments within bullet-list items.
The final conjunction-boundary comma is governed by the separate Oxford-comma check.
Does not require commas at the ends of bullet-list items.
rules.why: G-1 selects the list child rather than its grouping heading; G-4 selects the precise body wording; the grain test reserves the final boundary for the Oxford-comma check.

rules.quote: Do not punctuate the end of a list item with a comma if it is in a bullet list.
rules.violation_condition: A bullet-list item ends with a comma used as its terminal punctuation.
when: Applies to the ends of bullet-list items, not commas separating material within an item.
rules.why: The grain test separates an unwanted item-ending comma from a missing separator inside a sentence list.
